idiom_name: algebra interface generic in F + Kind<F, A> HKT emulation (Higher-Kinded-J) or per-effect dictionaries
implementation_notes: Java's generics are first-order and erased, so the `F[_]` of the Scala encoding cannot be written directly: `interface Console<F> { F<Unit> putLine(String s); }` is not valid Java. The workable realizations are (a) hand-written HKT emulation - a `Kind<F, A>` wrapper with a marker per effect, as provided by Higher-Kinded-J on Java 25+ - and (b) fixing the effect and injecting the algebra as an object, i.e. the program is generic in the algebra but not in the effect. What replaces the classic structure: an explicit dictionary object plus unchecked casts in the HKT layer, because Java resolves nothing implicitly and erases type arguments at run time. Manual support is justified when several interpretations of one domain must stay swappable and the team accepts the wrapper cost.
pitfalls: Type erasure removes the type argument at run time, so the HKT wrapper needs unchecked casts; a dictionary bound to the wrong effect compiles and fails late.
No implicit resolution: the dictionary is threaded manually or through a DI container, which is where Java's tagless final usually collapses back into plain injection.
`Unit` does not exist in Java - invent one (Higher-Kinded-J ships one) and keep it consistent, or void returns will not compose with the Kind wrapper.
Wildcards (`? extends`) and the Kind encoding interact badly: composing `Kind<F, ? extends A>` requires helper methods, so the algebra drifts away from the clear Scala form.
Preview features and a JDK floor come with the HKT library - check the toolchain before designing around it.
